title: Bast AI evidence library
source: Copied verbatim from the Bast research canvas 'Bast AI evidence library: explainability, caregiving, who pays' (checked October 28, 2026). Internal usage notes and internal planning sections are intentionally not in this public repo. studyType is a grouping derived from designAndSize for filtering; designAndSize is the verbatim text.

A.label: AI that shows its work keeps people thinking instead of offloading

B.label: Easing caregiver and care-worker burden improves patient outcomes

strengthDefinitions.Strong: An RCT, a randomized experiment or a meta-analysis of trials.
strengthDefinitions.Moderate: A cohort, reader study, quasi-experiment or review of observational studies.
strengthDefinitions.Limited: A survey, qualitative study, narrative review or self-report.
strengthDefinitions.Policy fact: Shows who pays, not whether something works.
strengthDefinitions.Vendor / unreviewed: Published by a vendor; not peer-reviewed.

directionDefinitions.Complicates: Cuts against it or limits it.

studies.title: LLMs alone vs people using LLMs
studies.finding: Tested alone, LLMs named the relevant condition in 94.9% of cases. Members of the public using the same LLMs got there in fewer than 34.5%, and picked the right next step in fewer than 44.2%. That was no better than a control group using their usual sources (the control group was better at naming conditions).
studies.designAndSize: Randomized, preregistered study; 1,298 UK adults; 10 medical scenarios; GPT-4o, Llama 3, Command R+
studies.caveats: Written scenarios, not real patients. Lay public, not clinicians. It tests the human-AI handoff, not explainability directly. 'Field' here means a person using the tool, not a hospital rollout.

studies.title: Neonatal X-ray AI: experts vs trainees
studies.finding: With a reliable-looking AI, radiology residents accepted 52.0% (13/25) of its wrong calls, vs 20.0% for pediatric radiologists and 33.3% for neonatologists. With a deliberately flawed AI, neonatologists overrode 91.7% (66/72) of its errors.
studies.source: Lee et al., npj Digital Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Multi-reader crossover reader study; 14 readers; 125 radiographs from 11 hospitals; 1,750 reads
studies.caveats: Only 3 neonatologists; authors call the 91.7% hypothesis-generating. Retrospective, web-based, one diagnosis. 91.7% and 52.0% measure different things (see section above). Group table is from the authors' repo.

studies.title: Colonoscopy deskilling
studies.finding: After endoscopists started using AI, their adenoma detection rate in colonoscopies done without AI fell from 28.4% to 22.4% (a 6.0-point drop).
studies.source: Budzyń et al., Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology
studies.designAndSize: Multicentre observational before/after; 1,443 non-AI colonoscopies in Poland
studies.caveats: Observational before/after, so it cannot prove AI caused the drop; other things changed over time. An erratum was published.

studies.title: Mammography automation bias
studies.finding: When the AI suggested the wrong BI-RADS category, correct ratings fell from 79.7% to 19.8% for inexperienced readers, 81.3% to 24.8% for moderately experienced, and 82.3% to 45.5% for very experienced radiologists.
studies.designAndSize: Prospective reader experiment; 27 radiologists; 50 mammograms
studies.caveats: Small sample. The 'AI' was simulated (researchers set its suggestions). Lab reading, not live screening.

studies.title: BCG 'jagged frontier'
studies.finding: On 18 tasks inside AI's abilities, consultants with GPT-4 did 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, with over 40% higher quality; below-average performers gained 43%, above-average 17%. On a task just outside AI's abilities, AI users were 19 percentage points less likely to get it right.
studies.source: Dell'Acqua et al., HBS working paper 24-013 (later published in Organization Science)
studies.designAndSize: Preregistered randomized field experiment; 758 BCG consultants
studies.caveats: Consulting tasks, GPT-4 in 2023, one firm. Quality was graded by people.

studies.title: Epic Sepsis Model, external validation
studies.finding: The widely used proprietary sepsis model had an AUC of 0.63, missed 67% of sepsis cases (1,709 of 2,552), and still alerted on 18% of all hospitalized patients.
studies.source: Wong et al., JAMA Internal Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Retrospective cohort; 27,697 patients, 38,455 hospitalizations at Michigan Medicine
studies.caveats: One health system; sepsis definitions vary between studies.

studies.title: Sepsis model before clinicians act
studies.finding: The same sepsis model scored AUROC 0.62 overall but 0.47 (worse than a coin flip) once predictions made after clinicians had already recognized sepsis were removed.
studies.designAndSize: Retrospective cohort; 77,582 hospitalizations
studies.caveats: One health system; retrospective.

studies.title: Google diabetic retinopathy AI in Thailand
studies.finding: In the first six months in Thai clinics, 393 of 1,838 eye images (21%) were rejected as ungradable, driven by lighting, no dilation drops and equipment problems.
studies.designAndSize: Field observation and interviews with nurses in 11 clinics
studies.caveats: Qualitative field study, not an accuracy trial. Lab accuracy figures are not reported in the same study.

studies.title: Pneumonia X-ray model across hospitals
studies.finding: A chest X-ray pneumonia model scored AUC 0.931 inside its own hospitals but 0.815 at an outside hospital. The models could tell which hospital an image came from (99.95% for NIH images).
studies.designAndSize: Cross-sectional study; 158,323 radiographs from 3 hospital systems
studies.caveats: Older models; retrospective.

studies.title: Dermatology AI on diverse skin
studies.finding: Three published skin-cancer models dropped from reported ROC-AUCs of 0.88 to 0.94 down to 0.56 to 0.67 on a new, biopsy-confirmed diverse image set, and did worst on dark skin.
studies.designAndSize: Retrospective evaluation on the DDI dataset (diverse skin tones)
studies.caveats: Image test set, not a clinical deployment. Fine-tuning on diverse images closed the skin-tone gap.

studies.title: How FDA-cleared AI is tested
studies.finding: 126 of 130 FDA-cleared AI devices (2015 to 2020) were evaluated only on retrospective data; none of the 54 high-risk devices had a prospective study; 93 reported no multi-site evaluation.
studies.designAndSize: Review of FDA summaries for 130 devices
studies.caveats: Based on public FDA summaries; devices through 2020.

studies.title: Explanations did not rescue a biased model
studies.finding: Clinician accuracy was 73.0% at baseline; a normal AI raised it 2.9 points (4.4 with explanations). A systematically biased AI cut it 11.3 points, and adding image explanations only partly helped (9.1-point drop; the 2.3-point difference was not significant).
studies.designAndSize: Randomized clinical vignette study; 457 hospitalists, NPs and PAs
studies.caveats: Vignettes, not live care. Tested heat-map style image explanations only.

studies.title: Explanations raised blind acceptance
studies.finding: Explanations made people more likely to accept the AI's answer whether it was right or wrong. Accuracy rose when the AI was right, fell when it was wrong, and team accuracy was no better than just showing the AI's confidence.
studies.designAndSize: Randomized online experiments; about 1,600 crowd workers; 3 tasks
studies.caveats: Lay tasks (review sentiment, LSAT questions), not clinical.

studies.title: Cognitive forcing (useful friction)
studies.finding: Asking people to decide first, request the AI, or wait cut over-reliance compared with simple explanations: when the AI was wrong, following it fell from 64% to 48% and correct answers rose from 8% to 27% (carb-source task). People liked these designs less.
studies.designAndSize: Randomized online experiment; 199 participants; nutrition task
studies.caveats: Lay task, simulated AI. Forcing reduced but did not remove over-reliance. Helped people high in 'need for cognition' most.

studies.title: When explanations do help
studies.finding: Explanations reduced over-reliance when they made checking the AI cheaper than trusting it; hard-to-read explanations did not help.
studies.designAndSize: 5 randomized online studies; 731 participants; maze task
studies.caveats: Lab task with a simulated AI.

studies.title: Annotated AI advice helps non-specialists
studies.finding: AI advice with a visual annotation on the X-ray produced the highest diagnostic accuracy, and physicians who were not task experts benefited the most.
studies.designAndSize: Randomized online experiment; 223 physicians (117 IM/EM, 106 radiology)
studies.caveats: All advice was correct, so it does not test whether annotations help people catch AI errors.

studies.title: Skin cancer: who gains, who gets misled
studies.finding: Good AI support beat AI or physicians alone, and the least experienced clinicians gained the most. Faulty AI misled clinicians at every level, including experts.
studies.designAndSize: Reader studies across expertise levels
studies.caveats: Reader studies on images, not live care.

studies.title: Experience doesn't predict who benefits
studies.finding: Across 140 radiologists and 15 chest X-ray tasks, years of experience, subspecialty and AI familiarity did not reliably predict who benefited from AI. Wrong AI predictions hurt performance.
studies.designAndSize: Large reader study; 140 radiologists
studies.caveats: Reader study, not live care.

studies.title: AI tutors with and without guardrails
studies.finding: Students with plain GPT-4 did 48% better in practice but 17% worse on a later exam without AI than students who never had it. A tutor version with guardrails lifted practice 127% and largely avoided the harm.
studies.designAndSize: Randomized field experiment; nearly 1,000 high school math students
studies.caveats: Education, not healthcare; one country and subject.

studies.title: Customer support: novices vs experts
studies.finding: An AI assistant raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average, 34% for novice and low-skilled agents, with minimal impact on experienced agents.
studies.source: Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond, NBER (published in QJE 2025)
studies.designAndSize: Staggered rollout, quasi-experimental; 5,179 support agents
studies.caveats: Productivity, not accuracy or learning. Numbers are from the NBER working paper; the 2025 journal version's figures may differ slightly.

studies.title: Confidence in AI and critical thinking
studies.finding: Knowledge workers with more confidence in GenAI reported less critical thinking; those with more self-confidence reported more.
studies.designAndSize: Survey; 319 knowledge workers; 936 real work examples
studies.caveats: Self-report, cross-sectional. Correlation only.

studies.title: MASAI mammography trial (AI that worked)
studies.finding: AI-supported screening found 6.1 vs 5.1 cancers per 1,000 women, with the same 1.5% false-positive rate and 44.3% less radiologist reading.
studies.designAndSize: Randomized controlled trial; 80,033 women in Sweden
studies.caveats: Interim safety analysis; the interval-cancer endpoint came later.

studies.title: Kansas Zemplee / Windsor Place pilot
studies.finding: 121 Medicaid members who qualified for nursing-home care but lived at home: nursing-facility days fell 54%, depression scores 45% and loneliness scores 29% vs before the pilot. Technology cost under $600 per person per month; 7 of 109 analyzed (about 6%) moved to a nursing home.
studies.source: Zemplee and Windsor Place At-Home Care press release (white paper 'Nursing Homes Without Walls')
studies.designAndSize: Single-arm pilot with before/after comparison; 121 people; partners KU Medical Center, UnitedHealthcare of Kansas; KDADS funding
studies.caveats: Preliminary, vendor-published, not peer-reviewed, no control group. Bundles sensors, vitals monitoring, devices and in-home services, so results can't be pinned on the AI.

studies.title: NYU Caregiver Intervention
studies.finding: Counseling and support for spouse caregivers cut the rate of nursing-home placement by 28.3% (HR 0.717) and delayed it by a model-predicted median of 557 days. Caregiver improvements explained 61.2% of the effect.
studies.designAndSize: Randomized controlled trial; 406 spouse caregivers of people with Alzheimer's; enrolled over 9.5 years
studies.caveats: Volunteer sample of spouse caregivers in one New York program; 557 days is a model-predicted median.

studies.title: REACH II
studies.finding: A 6-month, 12-session caregiver program improved caregiver quality of life and cut clinical depression (12.6% vs 22.7%). No significant difference in institutionalization at 6 months.
studies.source: Belle et al., Annals of Internal Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Randomized controlled trial; 642 Hispanic, white and Black caregivers in 5 US cities
studies.caveats: Only 6-month follow-up; too short to show placement effects.

studies.title: Caregiver mental health and patient survival
studies.finding: Worse caregiver mental health predicted higher patient mortality, even after accounting for diagnosis, age, sex, dementia severity and the patient's own mental health.
studies.designAndSize: Prospective cohort; 176 patient-caregiver dyads with neurodegenerative disease
studies.caveats: Small, one center. Association, not proof of cause.

studies.title: Caregiver strain and caregiver mortality
studies.finding: Older spousal caregivers who felt strain had a 63% higher risk of dying over 4 years than non-caregivers (RR 1.63). Caregivers without strain had no higher risk.
studies.source: Schulz & Beach, JAMA (Caregiver Health Effects Study)
studies.designAndSize: Prospective cohort of older adults; 4-year follow-up
studies.caveats: Observational; confidence interval touches 1.00.

studies.title: What predicts nursing-home admission
studies.finding: Across 80 studies, caregivers' emotional stress, wish to institutionalize and feeling 'trapped' predicted nursing-home admission for people with dementia, alongside patient factors.
studies.designAndSize: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 80 studies
studies.caveats: Pooled observational studies; predictors, not causes.

studies.title: Caregiver burden and ED returns
studies.finding: Each 1-point rise on the Zarit burden scale was linked to 3% higher odds of an ED revisit within 30 days (OR 1.03). No link at 3 or 7 days, or for revisits ending in admission.
studies.source: JAMA Network Open (LEARNING WISDOM cohort, Québec)
studies.designAndSize: Prospective cohort; 1,409 patient-caregiver dyads (patients 65+)
studies.caveats: Small effect with a confidence interval starting at 1.00; COVID-era data.

studies.title: Caregivers in discharge planning
studies.finding: Bringing family caregivers into discharge planning cut readmissions by 25% at 90 days (RR 0.75) and 24% at 180 days (RR 0.76).
studies.source: Rodakowski et al., Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
studies.designAndSize: Meta-analysis; 15 studies (11 with readmission data)
studies.caveats: Interventions varied a lot between studies.

studies.title: BRI Care Consultation (Benjamin Rose)
studies.finding: Caregivers had 21% fewer depression symptoms at 12 months (Kaiser trial). In the VA version, caregiver depression symptoms rose 6.8% vs 28.2%, and veterans with more behavioral symptoms had fewer readmissions (1.7 vs 2.5) and fewer return ED visits (2.5 vs 3.5).
studies.source: US Administration for Community Living program summary
studies.designAndSize: One RCT (Kaiser Permanente) and one matched-site trial (VA Partners in Dementia Care, 328 veterans)
studies.caveats: Use effects showed up only in subgroups; no difference in the chance of any admission or ED visit.

studies.title: Nurse staffing and patient death (US)
studies.finding: Each extra patient per nurse was linked to 7% higher odds of a surgical patient dying within 30 days (OR 1.07) and 23% higher odds of nurse burnout (OR 1.23).
studies.designAndSize: Cross-sectional linked data; 10,184 nurses, 232,342 patients, 168 Pennsylvania hospitals
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional; association, not cause.

studies.title: Nurse staffing and death (Europe)
studies.finding: One more patient per nurse raised the odds of in-hospital death within 30 days by 7%; every 10% more bachelor's-trained nurses lowered it by 7%.
studies.designAndSize: Retrospective observational; hospitals in 9 European countries
studies.caveats: Observational.

studies.title: Physician burnout and patient safety
studies.finding: Burned-out physicians had about twice the odds of patient safety incidents (OR 1.96), lower professionalism (OR 2.31) and lower patient satisfaction (OR 2.28).
studies.source: Panagioti et al., JAMA Internal Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Meta-analysis; 47 studies, 42,473 physicians
studies.caveats: High heterogeneity; low-to-moderate study quality; much is self-reported.

studies.title: Patients forget most of what's said
studies.finding: 40% to 80% of medical information from clinicians is forgotten immediately, and almost half of what is remembered is wrong.
studies.source: Kessels, Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Narrative review
studies.caveats: Figures come from older underlying studies, not new data.

studies.title: Medicare GUIDE model
studies.finding: Medicare pays for dementia care navigation, a 24/7 support line, caregiver training and education, and respite services up to $2,500 a year, in an 8-year model that started July 2024.
studies.designAndSize: Federal payment model (program page)
studies.caveats: Dementia only; available only through participating programs. Shows a payer pays, not what it pays for an app.

studies.title: Medicare pays for caregiver training
studies.finding: From 2024, Medicare pays when practitioners train caregivers to help carry out a patient's treatment plan (for example, in dementia).
studies.source: CMS, CY 2024 Physician Fee Schedule final rule fact sheet
studies.designAndSize: Federal payment rule
studies.caveats: Paid to clinicians, not to apps or caregivers.

studies.title: Medicaid pays family caregivers
studies.finding: All responding states pay family caregivers through at least one Medicaid home care program, and all cover respite; 44 states allow paying legally responsible relatives through waivers.
studies.designAndSize: Survey of state Medicaid programs (all states but Florida responded)
studies.caveats: Benefits are optional and may shrink after 2025 federal Medicaid cuts.

studies.title: What dementia caregivers would pay
studies.finding: 57% of dementia caregivers would pay something for an 8-session in-home program; mean adjusted willingness was $36 per session. Each extra hour of daily help raised it $1.64.
studies.designAndSize: Willingness-to-pay survey at baseline of an RCT; 226 caregivers
studies.caveats: Stated, not actual, payment; 32% said $0 and 11% refused to answer.

studies.title: Adult Day Services Plus: will vs able to pay
studies.finding: Median willingness to pay was $90 to $100 per session, but ability to pay was $31.50 to $50. The program cost $433 per dyad a year; payer savings of $1,501 were not statistically significant.
studies.source: Pizzi et al., Innovation in Aging
studies.designAndSize: Cluster-randomized trial; 34 sites; 203 caregivers
studies.caveats: Savings not significant; stated willingness.

studies.title: France: value of an hour of care
studies.finding: Caregivers valued an hour of informal care at €12.10; needing care training was tied to higher value, needing respite or support groups was not.
studies.source: Gervès-Pinquié et al., Health Economics Review
studies.designAndSize: Contingent valuation from national surveys; 223 Alzheimer's caregivers
studies.caveats: 2008 data; French setting; cross-sectional.

studies.title: Caregivers already pay a lot
studies.finding: Family caregivers spend an average of $7,242 a year out of pocket, about 26% of their income ($8,978 for dementia caregivers).
studies.designAndSize: National survey with a diary component
studies.caveats: Survey; most spending is housing and medical.

studies.title: Employers lose caregivers
studies.finding: 32% of employees had voluntarily left a job because of caregiving responsibilities.
studies.source: Fuller & Raman, The Caring Company (Harvard Business School)
studies.designAndSize: Employee and employer surveys; over 1,500 employees
studies.caveats: Survey; self-reported.
